Stack.summary: A last-in, first-out stack whose elements can also be read by index.
Stack.description:
A Stack keeps its elements in the order they were pushed: push adds one on top, pop removes the one on top. Indexes count from the bottom, as in an array: stack[0] is the first element pushed, stack[stack.length - 1] the top, and an index without an element reads undefined.

Indexes are only for reading: the stack changes only through push and pop. A stack cannot be iterated or spread either: loop on values, a copy of its elements.

Xaendar uses it where a nested operation, once it ends, must restore the state it interrupted: the states of the lexer of the compiler, and the computations in progress in the signals runtime.

members.length: The number of elements in the stack.
members.values: A copy of the elements, from the bottom to the top: changing it does not change the stack. Every read makes a new copy.
members.push: Adds an element on top of the stack and returns the new length.
members.pop: Removes the element on top of the stack and returns it, or returns undefined when the stack is empty.

pushingAndPopping.title: Pushing, reading and popping
pushingAndPopping.body: The tags opened and not closed yet, as a parser keeps them: the innermost tag is on top, and closing it pops it.

toPascalCase.summary: Converts a kebab-case, snake_case or camelCase string to PascalCase.
toPascalCase.description:
Removes every - and _ and upper-cases the character that follows it, then upper-cases the first character. Nothing else changes: the other letters keep their case, so 'USER-CARD' becomes 'USERCARD', and spaces and dots stay where they are.

The CLI uses it to name the class of a component after its selector: xd g c user-card declares UserCardComponent. See CLI.

converting.title: Converting names
converting.body: The three conventions give the same result, and a name in capitals stays in capitals.

toKebabCase.summary: Converts a camelCase, PascalCase or snake_case string to kebab-case.
toKebabCase.description:
Puts a - between a lowercase letter and the uppercase letter that follows it, replaces every _ with -, then lower-cases the whole string.

Only a lowercase letter followed by an uppercase one starts a new word: a run of capitals, as in an acronym, is not split, and neither is a digit followed by a capital. 'parseXML' becomes 'parse-xml', but 'XMLParser' becomes 'xmlparser'. Spaces are kept.

For names made of lowercase words it undoes toPascalCase: toKebabCase(toPascalCase('user-card')) is 'user-card'.

converting.title: Converting names
converting.body: Class and property names become names in the style of custom elements and CSS classes.

indent.summary: Indents a line, or each line of an array, by two spaces.
indent.description:
Prepends two spaces to a string, or to each string of an array. An array gives a new array, and the one passed in is left as it is. Empty lines are indented too. The compiler uses it to indent the code it generates, one level per call.

A string is treated as one line: when it contains line breaks, only its first line is indented. Split it first, and pass the array.

indenting.title: Indenting generated code
indenting.body: Each call adds one level, two spaces, to what it receives. A block in one string is split into lines first.

isNonEmpty.summary: Checks whether an object has at least one own enumerable property, and narrows its type when it does.
isNonEmpty.description:
Returns true when Object.keys(object) is not empty: when the object has at least one own enumerable property with a string key. A property holding undefined counts; inherited properties, non-enumerable ones and symbol keys do not.

It is a type guard: where it returns true, the object has the type NonEmptyObject<Obj> of type-fest. A type whose keys are all optional becomes a type requiring at least one of them, as RequireOne does, and a type with a required key stays as it is. The guard reads the keys, not the values: an object whose only key holds undefined passes it.

Arrays are objects: [] is empty, [0] is not. A Map or a Set keeps its entries outside its properties, so they do not count: check its size.

narrowing.title: Requiring at least one filter
narrowing.body: A function needing at least one of some optional keys declares its parameter with RequireOne. An object of the plain type does not fit it, until isNonEmpty has checked it.

isEmpty.summary: Checks whether an object has no own enumerable properties.
isEmpty.description:
The opposite of isNonEmpty: returns true when Object.keys(object) is empty. The same properties count: own, enumerable, with a string key, even when they hold undefined. The entries of a Map or a Set are not properties, so they do not count.

It is not a type guard: it returns a plain boolean, and the type of the object does not change.

whatCounts.title: What counts as empty
whatCounts.body: The result follows Object.keys, for arrays, maps and symbol keys too.

keys.summary: Returns the own enumerable property names of an object, typed with the keys of its type.
keys.description:
Calls Object.keys and types the result as an array of the keys of the type of the object, instead of string[], so each name can index the object without a cast. Called with undefined, it returns undefined.

The type trusts the object: properties it does not declare are returned anyway, and numeric keys are typed as strings, as Object.keys always returns them: keys({ 1: 'one' }) is ['1'], typed '1'[].

A value typed as an object or undefined is accepted too: the result is then typed as an array or undefined.

typedKeys.title: Typed keys
typedKeys.body: The names come back typed with the keys of the object, so a loop over them reads its values without a cast.

entries.summary: Returns the own enumerable [key, value] pairs of an object, typed with the keys and the values of its type.
entries.description:
Calls Object.entries and types each pair as [Key, Value]: a key of the type of the object, where Object.entries gives string, and its values, where Object.entries gives any for an interface or a class. Called with undefined, it returns undefined.

The key and the value of a pair are typed separately: for { id: number; name: string } a pair is ['id' | 'name', string | number], so checking the key does not narrow the value. As with keys, the type trusts the object, numeric keys are typed as strings, and a value typed as an object or undefined is accepted.

typedPairs.title: Typed pairs
typedPairs.body: The pairs are destructured in the loop, the name typed with the keys of the theme.

values.summary: Returns the own enumerable property values of an object, typed with the values of its type.
values.description:
Calls Object.values and types the result with the values of the type of the object, a union when they differ. Object.values infers the same for an object literal type, but gives any[] for an interface or a class. Called with undefined, it returns undefined.

As with keys, the type trusts the object, and a value typed as an object or undefined is accepted.

typedValues.title: Typed values
typedValues.body: The values come back typed, ready for the array methods.

removeItem.summary: Removes the first occurrence of an item from an array, in place, and tells whether it found it.
removeItem.description:
Looks for the item with indexOf, so with ===, and removes it with splice: the array passed in changes, and nothing is copied. Only the first occurrence goes; the others stay. Returns true when the item was removed, false when the array does not contain it.

NaN is never found, since NaN === NaN is false.

removing.title: Removing an item
removing.body: The array changes in place, and the result tells whether the item was there.

slice.summary: Extracts a part of a string as a new string, which does not keep the original in memory.
slice.description:
Returns the same characters as value.slice(start, end), with the same indexes: start included, end excluded, a negative index counted from the end, a missing one meaning the start or the end of the string.

The difference is in memory. V8, the engine of Chrome and Node.js, can return the result of String.prototype.slice as a view on the original string, a sliced string, which keeps the whole original alive as long as the part is. slice copies the part through JSON.stringify and JSON.parse, so the result owns its characters and the original can be garbage collected.

The compiler and the Vite plugin use it for the parts of a source they keep after reading it: names, expressions, texts. The copy has a cost, worth paying for short parts that outlive a long string.

keepingAPart.title: Keeping a part of a long string
keepingAPart.body: The indexes work as in String.prototype.slice. The name kept from the source does not hold the source.

isValidCustomElementName.summary: Checks whether a string can be the name of a custom element, and logs why when it cannot.
isValidCustomElementName.description:
A name is valid when it:

  • starts with a lowercase ASCII letter;
  • contains a hyphen;
  • contains only lowercase ASCII letters, digits, -, ., _ and most non-ASCII characters, such as é or α, as the HTML specification allows; never an uppercase ASCII letter, a space or another ASCII symbol;
  • is not one of the names reserved by the HTML specification: annotation-xml, color-profile, font-face, font-face-src, font-face-uri, font-face-format, font-face-name, missing-glyph.

These are the rules of the specification, the ones customElements.define applies: a name is valid here exactly when it is valid for the browser. The reserved names are the SVG and MathML elements with a hyphen; the other native elements have none, so their names are never valid.

An invalid name returns false: nothing is thrown. The Vite plugin checks with it the selector of every component, and the CLI the name of a new component (xd g c) and of the root component of a new project (xd new): both print its message when a name is invalid. See Selectors and registration.

members.tagName: The name to check, as it is: it is neither trimmed nor lower-cased, so a space or a capital letter makes it invalid.
members.logErrors: Whether to print with console.error why the name is invalid, with the rules or the reserved names. The compiler passes false to tell the custom elements of a template from the native elements without printing anything.

checking.title: Valid and invalid names
checking.body: Each name is checked as written, against the rules above.

matchesCustomElementPattern.summary: Checks whether a tag name matches at least one of a list of patterns, where * stands for any sequence of characters.
matchesCustomElementPattern.description:
A pattern matches the whole tag name. * stands for any sequence of characters, hyphens and the empty sequence included, so sl-* matches sl-button and sl-icon-button, but not xsl-button. Every other character matches only itself, case included: a . is a dot, not any character. With no patterns, the result is false.

The patterns are the ones of customElements in xaendar.json: the compiler uses this function to recognize the tags of the custom elements of other libraries, which it treats as native elements. See Selectors and registration.

otherLibraries.title: Matching the tags of other libraries
otherLibraries.body: A list as customElements declares it: a pattern for a whole library, and the name of a single element.
